strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: performance collapse in LLM-based multi-agent systems when the agent pool is expanded and the router cold-starts on new agents. Figure 1 and the additional Table 3 results (e.g., Gemini-3-Pro dropping by 13% at 7 agents) provide convincing empirical evidence that this failure mode is real, even for strong proprietary routers.

The theoretical contribution is clean and internally consistent: casting sequential MAS expansion as a stage-wise contextual bandit, defining a conservative policy lift to bridge action-space changes across stages, and proving a monotonic non-degradation guarantee via a TRPO-style trust-region surrogate. The proofs (Lemma 4.1, 4.2, Theorem 4.3) are correct given the stated assumptions.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation across two benchmarks (GAIA, HLE) and two agent-pool regimes (clean and malfunctioning), showing that the proposed memory-based method scales more stably than naive scale-up and can let a smaller open-weight router (Qwen-3-30B) approach or exceed larger proprietary-router baselines.

Detailed appendices (agent cards, prompts, memory schema, case studies) substantially aid reproducibility and give useful qualitative insight into failure modes (cold-start misjudgment, brittle workflow handovers) and how memory-guided routing corrects them.

The malfunctioning-agent-pool experiment is a valuable robustness stress test that other papers in this space typically omit, and shows a genuinely interesting result: pass@3 alone does not rescue a strong router from noisy-pool collapse, whereas the proposed familiarization+memory approach does.
weaknesses: There is a non-trivial gap between the theoretical guarantee and what is actually implemented. The monotonicity proof rests on Assumption B.2, that the conservative fallback memory exactly realizes the lifted policy, and on the trust-region update exactly solving an argmax over the surrogate objective with an exact KL constraint. In practice, memory candidates are generated by an LLM-based distillation process and the update rule is described only qualitatively ("select a safe update"); it is unclear how (or whether) the KL divergence between two LLM-conditioned routing policies is estimated/enforced in the actual system. This makes the theorem more of a design rationale than a verified guarantee for the deployed system, and this gap is not explicitly discussed as a limitation.

No variance, multiple seeds, or statistical significance reporting for the main GAIA/HLE results, despite GAIA validation being a modest-sized benchmark (~165 examples) where a few points of accuracy could plausibly be attributable to sampling noise in LLM-based routing/execution. This weakens confidence in the reported monotonic trends, especially the smaller per-stage gains (e.g., 44.84%→47.27%).

Comparisons are limited to naive scale-up and fixed-pool SOTA-router baselines; the paper does not compare against other adaptive/memory-based agent-learning methods cited in its own related work (e.g., ReasoningBank, Training-Free GRPO, dynamic LLM routing methods such as ICL-Router or Avengers), so it is hard to gauge how much of the improvement is attributable to the specific trust-region/conservative-fallback design versus generic experience accumulation.

MonoScale is only evaluated with a single router backbone (Qwen-3-30B-A3B-Instruct); it is unclear whether the method transfers to other backbones or whether gains would hold if a stronger backbone were equipped with the same memory mechanism, which would strengthen the claim that "adaptive router updates—rather than backbone strength alone—are crucial."

Scale of experiments (agent pools up to N=10) is small relative to the paper's stated motivation ("Agentic Web" with potentially millions of agents); this is honestly acknowledged in the Discussion, but it does leave open whether the trust-region/memory mechanism remains tractable and effective at realistic scale (e.g., memory length budget K, candidate generation cost growing with pool size).

The familiarization stage uses a fairly small warm-up set (~50 synthesized tasks per new agent, 4 samples each), and the paper does not analyze sensitivity of results to this budget or report how often the identity/no-update fallback is triggered in practice, which would help substantiate the claimed conservativeness of the method.

strengths: Addresses a clearly motivated and practically important problem: cold-start-induced performance collapse when a multi-agent system's router must accommodate newly added, heterogeneous agents. Figure 1 provides a clean, striking empirical demonstration of the failure mode that motivates the work.

The overall framework (agent-conditioned warm-up task synthesis + evidence-driven natural-language memory update with a conservative fallback) is intuitive, practically actionable, and clearly described with an explicit algorithm (Algorithm 1) and memory schema (Appendix E), aiding reproducibility.

Experiments are fairly comprehensive: main results on GAIA and HLE across agent-pool sizes 3-10 (and a 20-agent probe), an ablation isolating the contribution of negative memory and customized warm-up, a cross-router memory-transfer study showing the distilled memory is not backbone-specific, a noisy/malfunctioning-agent-pool robustness study, and a multi-seed variance analysis - together giving a fairly complete empirical picture.

The paper is candid about limitations, including the conditional nature of the monotonicity guarantee, the small-scale (≤20 agent) validation relative to the 'Agentic Web' framing, and a local non-monotonic dip in the empirical curve, which it investigates rather than hiding (Appendix D.7).

Detailed case studies (Appendix F) illustrate concrete failure modes (cold-start capability misjudgment, brittle interface mismatches, confirmation bias) and how memory retrieval resolves them, adding interpretability to the quantitative results.
weaknesses: The theoretical monotonicity guarantee (Theorem 4.3) is largely definitional/by-construction: because the conservative fallback memory is always included in the candidate set and trivially satisfies the KL constraint (KL=0), the 'proof' essentially restates that an optimizer which can always choose to do nothing cannot do worse than doing nothing. This is a much weaker theoretical contribution than the framing ('monotonic improvement guarantee') suggests, and it does not certify that the deployed heuristic candidate-selection procedure (Algorithm 1, which uses LLM-based semantic consistency checks rather than a verifiable KL computation) actually satisfies the stated assumptions in practice.

There is a gap between the deployed 'practical instantiation' (one-shot conservative selection over LLM-distilled candidates) and the theoretical trust-region optimization it is claimed to instantiate; no formal argument or empirical measurement is given that the LLM-based semantic trust region reliably approximates the KL constraint used in the proof.

Empirical scale (up to 10, with a single 20-agent probe) is far short of the motivating narrative of 'catalogs containing thousands to millions of agents' in an 'Agentic Web'; the paper acknowledges this but the gap between motivation and demonstrated scalability is substantial, and it is unclear whether the natural-language memory approach remains tractable (context length, retrieval, conflict resolution) at even moderate scales beyond 20 agents.

The full MonoScale method (task synthesis + memory update) is only evaluated with a single open-weight router backbone (Qwen-3-30B-A3B-Instruct); the claim that 'adaptive router updates rather than backbone strength alone are crucial' would be more convincing if MonoScale were also applied to at least one additional backbone in the main results (the cross-router transfer study only tests transferring Qwen-generated memory to Gemini-3-Flash, not generating memory natively with a second backbone as a controlled comparison in the main tables).

The synthetic agent pool (camel-ai-based, hand-crafted malfunctioning agents with specific injected failure modes) is somewhat artificial; it is unclear how representative these failure modes are of real-world heterogeneous, third-party agents, and whether the warm-up/memory approach generalizes to failure modes not anticipated by the paper's design.

Several baseline models referenced (e.g., GPT-5.2, Gemini-3-Pro, DeepSeek-V3.2) appear to be near-future or fast-moving proprietary systems; reliance on such APIs raises reproducibility concerns since their behavior/availability may change, and exact experimental conditions (temperature, exact model snapshots) are not fully specified in the main text.

Variance analysis is conducted only on a 40-task GAIA subset with 3 seeds, which is a small sample for assessing the stability of reported percentage-point differences (e.g., several ablation and comparison deltas are within a few points, comparable in magnitude to the measured variance).

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and practically relevant problem: cold-start performance collapse when scaling multi-agent systems, backed by a convincing motivating experiment (Figure 1) showing real performance collapse across multiple router backbones.

The contextual-bandit formalization and trust-region/conservative-fallback framing is clean, and the paper is unusually thorough in stress-testing its own assumptions empirically (Appendix C.2 validates the non-interfering expansion assumption via decision-overlap and reward-stability checks).

Extensive supplementary experiments: ablations isolating negative memory vs. customized warm-up (Table 4), cross-router memory transfer (Table 5), scaling beyond 10 agents, onboarding cost analysis, multi-seed variance checks, and a noisy/malfunctioning agent pool study, going beyond what is typical in this line of work.

Detailed, transparent case studies (Appendix F) that concretely illustrate the failure modes (cold-start misjudgment, brittle workflow links) and how memory retrieval resolves them, aiding interpretability of the mechanism.
High reproducibility effort: full agent cards, prompts, malfunctioning-agent specifications, and memory schema are documented in the appendix.
weaknesses: The headline empirical claim ('MonoScale ... can even outperform the strong-router + fixed agent pool baseline') is undercut by the paper's own appendix: Table 3 shows Gemini-3-Pro at 5 agents (no memory mechanism at all) reaches 65.45% GAIA accuracy, substantially higher than MonoScale's best reported 55.15% at 10 agents. The main-text comparison in Table 1 restricts strong-model baselines to 3 agents only, which, combined with the deferred and less prominent appendix table showing a stronger competing configuration, gives a presentation that is more favorable to the proposed method than the full evidence supports.

The theoretical monotonicity guarantee (Theorem 4.3) is comparatively shallow: given that the candidate set always contains a fallback that is proven equal in value to the pre-expansion policy, the 'monotonic improvement' result reduces to 'the argmax over a set containing a zero-improvement option is at least zero-improvement,' which is close to a tautology rather than a substantive optimization guarantee. The paper does not show the practical algorithm actually finds improving updates beyond the trivial fallback with any guaranteed frequency.

There is an acknowledged gap between the theoretical trust-region optimization (Eq. 10-11, TRPO-style surrogate) and the deployed algorithm, which performs a one-shot heuristic selection over LLM-distilled candidates (Section 3.2.2, 'Practical instantiation'); no formal connection is established between the practical selection procedure's behavior and the surrogate objective's guarantees, so the theory's coverage of the actual system is limited.

Empirical monotonicity is not actually observed in the main results — there is a dip at N=6 in Figure 3, explained post hoc in Appendix D.7 as tool-budget exhaustion. While the explanation is plausible, it also means the flagship empirical narrative ('stable gains,' 'non-decreasing') requires qualification that is not evident from the abstract or main text.

Statistical robustness is thin for the primary results: Table 1/2 report single-run numbers (no seeds/variance) on relatively small benchmarks (GAIA validation ~165 examples, with Level 3 subsets of only ~26 items), so multi-point percentage swings used to argue trends could be within noise; the multi-seed check (Appendix D.6) is run on only a 40-question subset rather than the full benchmark.

The comparison between MonoScale's 10-agent system and baselines' 3-agent systems conflates the benefit of a larger/more diverse tool pool with the benefit of better routing/memory, since baselines are not evaluated at matched agent-pool sizes in the main table (only in an appendix table that is de-emphasized and, as noted above, actually weakens the paper's claim).

The agent pool and 'malfunctioning agent' injections (Appendix A.3) are custom-built for this paper rather than drawn from an external/standardized benchmark, raising concerns about whether the reported failure modes and resulting gains generalize beyond this specific engineered testbed.

The warm-up task distribution is asserted to be 'a practical proxy' of the deployment distribution D without any quantitative validation of distributional similarity, which is a load-bearing but under-examined assumption given that the theoretical guarantee explicitly requires accurate expectation estimation under D.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: Figure 1 provides compelling empirical evidence of cold-start-induced performance collapse when scaling MAS agent pools across three different router backbones, grounding the paper's central claim before any method is introduced.

Rigorous theoretical contribution: the paper formalizes sequential agent-pool expansion as a stage-wise contextual bandit, introduces a conservative-lift construction to make cross-stage comparison well-defined, and proves a conditional monotonic non-degradation guarantee (Theorem 4.3) with complete, correct proofs in the appendix.

Thoughtful, auditable method design: the two-stage familiarization-and-memory-update protocol (agent-conditioned task synthesis + trust-region memory selection with an always-available conservative fallback) is a sensible and practically implementable instantiation of the theory, and the natural-language memory format is inspectable/rollbackable.

Extensive and multi-faceted empirical evaluation: main results on GAIA and HLE across N=3..10 agents, comparisons to strong proprietary routers, an ablation isolating negative-memory and customized-warm-up contributions, a noisy/malfunctioning agent-pool robustness study, cross-router memory-transfer experiments, multi-seed variance analysis, and onboarding cost accounting — this is unusually thorough for a systems-style contribution.

Honest treatment of limitations and assumptions: the paper explicitly validates (rather than just asserts) its non-interfering expansion assumption empirically (Appendix C.2), analyzes a local non-monotonic dip in the main curve (Appendix D.7) instead of hiding it, and clearly scopes claims about web-scale generalization as future work.
High reproducibility: full agent cards, system prompts, task-decomposition/assignment prompts, the memory schema (Appendix E), and the algorithmic procedure (Algorithm 1) are all provided in detail.
weaknesses: The theoretical monotonicity guarantee is heavily conditioned on the non-interfering expansion and feasible-fallback assumptions; the empirical validation of these assumptions is fairly thin (a single 100-question subset with a 2-point/not-significant accuracy gap), so the practical strength of the guarantee in less controlled deployments remains uncertain.

The core theoretical technique is largely an application of TRPO-style conservative policy-improvement ideas (bandit surrogate + trust region + safe fallback) to the memory-editing setting; the framing is novel but the underlying mathematical machinery is not fundamentally new.

The comparison methodology against strong-router baselines is somewhat asymmetric: MonoScale's 10-agent result is compared against strong-router 3-agent configurations rather than against strong routers equipped with an analogous memory-update mechanism at the same scale, and the paper's justification for this choice (non-monotonicity making a 'best' naive-scaled config unknowable a priori) is reasonable but still leaves open whether a memory-augmented strong router would outperform MonoScale even more.

Reported gains are sometimes close to the estimated variance: the multi-seed study (Appendix D.6) finds a standard deviation of ~1.4–2.9 points on a 40-task subset, which is non-trivial relative to some reported improvements (e.g., the 6.6% relative gain at 7 agents translates to a small absolute GAIA delta), so some individual data points should be interpreted cautiously.

Scalability claims beyond the tested range are aspirational rather than demonstrated: experiments only go up to 20 agents (a single preliminary probe), while the motivation section discusses catalogs of thousands to millions of agents; the paper appropriately flags this as future work, but it tempers the significance of the contribution for true web-scale settings.

The malfunctioning-agent pool is hand-constructed with specific, somewhat stylized failure modes (semantic mismatch, honey-pot exaggerated prompts, etc.), which may not fully capture the diversity of real-world agent unreliability encountered in production MAS.

Evaluation is limited to two benchmarks (GAIA and HLE-MCQ) and one MAS toolkit (camel-ai); generalization of the framework's benefits to other task domains, tool ecosystems, or agent-pool compositions is not empirically shown.
